questions.q: Why does the lesson say immediately solving a mentee's hard bug for them is 'usually the worst available option,' even though it's the fastest fix?
options: The specific bug gets fixed, but the mentee doesn't practice the transferable skill of systematically narrowing down a hard problem, leaving them less prepared for the next similar bug
Immediately solving the bug is always technically incorrect
There is no real downside to immediately solving a mentee's problem
Fast fixes are against company policy in every engineering organization
questions.explain: The mentee learns that THIS bug is fixed, but not HOW to find the next one like it -- the actual transferable skill (systematic debugging) never gets exercised when someone else does it for them.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend asking a 'narrowing question' (e.g., 'does this happen under concurrent load?') instead of directly naming the likely cause?
options: Narrowing questions guarantee the mentee will never make a mistake
Narrowing questions are always faster than just stating the answer
It points toward the real cause without stating it, and models the KIND of question a skilled debugger asks -- which is the actual transferable skill being taught
This technique only works for bugs involving concurrency
questions.explain: The value isn't just solving THIS bug faster -- it's demonstrating the reasoning process (what question would a skilled debugger ask here) that the mentee can reuse on a future, different problem.

questions.q: How does the lesson distinguish a moment that calls for a nudge from one where the mentor should just give the direct answer?
options: This distinction doesn't actually matter -- the same response is always correct
The mentor should never give a direct answer under any circumstances
The mentor should always give the direct answer immediately regardless of how long the mentee has been stuck

A mentee who's briefly stuck and hasn't tried an obvious angle usually benefits from a nudge; a mentee who's genuinely blocked, time-pressured, and has already tried everything is better served by a direct answer with the reasoning explained
questions.explain: Reading the real situation (a brief stuck moment vs. genuine, costly blockage) rather than defaulting to one fixed approach is explicitly named as part of the mentoring skill itself.

questions.q: Why might a mentor deliberately let a mentee implement an awkward or suboptimal fix rather than redirecting them immediately?
options: When the cost of the detour is genuinely low (a few hours, not a production incident), discovering the awkwardness firsthand can teach more than being told about it in advance
Letting mistakes happen is always better than preventing them, regardless of cost
This approach only applies to mentees who have already made the exact same mistake before
A mentor should never give any technical guidance under any circumstances
questions.explain: The lesson frames this as conditional on the detour being genuinely bounded in cost -- letting someone discover an issue themselves can build understanding, but only when the real cost of that detour stays low.

questions.q: What does the lesson say a mentor should do even when the situation genuinely calls for giving the direct answer?
options: Explain the reasoning that would have led there, not just the conclusion, so the next similar problem is a little more findable on the mentee's own
Give the answer with no explanation of how it was reached
Never explain anything, since explanations waste time in genuinely urgent situations
Always apologize for giving a direct answer instead of a nudge
questions.explain: Even when circumstances require just giving the answer, explaining the reasoning behind it preserves some of the learning value that a pure answer-with-no-explanation would lose entirely.
